title: The actor's longing
hook: Talaputa, an actor turned monk, talks to his own restless mind (Theragatha, Talaputa)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angulimala stopped, and the moon came out from the cloud. Your line was the moon from the cloud. Did you take one small next step? Today, a monk who keeps asking himself one word: when. Day eight hundred two.

When. It's a word for waiting rooms, long drives, the last hour before the weekend. In one of the long songs in the brothers' book, it's the word an actor says to himself over and over. Talaputa led a troupe of players. In a sutta, he asks the Buddha what becomes of actors who make crowds laugh with truth and lies. The Buddha would rather not answer, then does, and Talaputa weeps, and asks to go forth. In his song, he turns and talks to his own mind.
screen: `WHEN.` → `AN ACTOR ASKS ABOUT ACTORS.` → `HE TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: First, the longing. His song opens with a run of questions. When will I live alone in mountain caves? When will I wear the rag robe and want nothing? When will I see clearly that it all passes? When, when, when. The Pali word is kada, and it comes back so often it becomes the rhythm of the poem. Second, the turn. Further on, the questions stop, and he speaks to the mind directly, as if it were someone sitting across from him. You're the one who urged me into this life, he says, and now you pull the other way. Third, the tone. It isn't only scolding. He reasons with the mind. He coaxes it. He reminds it of the forest, the rain, the calling birds, the quiet it said it wanted. Some readers hear an actor's craft in it: one man playing two parts on one stage, the restless mind and the patient monk, trading lines. Fourth, what it means on an ordinary day. Talaputa doesn't pretend the restless mind belongs to someone else. He also doesn't simply do what it says. He talks to it like someone he has to live with, and will keep living with. His song doesn't pretend one talking-to settles it. Verse after verse, the longing stays honest, and the conversation goes on. Perhaps that's what an actor brought to the forest: the knack of hearing your own voice as one voice among several, and answering it.
screen: `A RUN OF QUESTIONS: WHEN?` · `HE SPEAKS TO THE MIND DIRECTLY.` · `SCOLDING, REASONING, COAXING.` · `TWO PARTS ON ONE STAGE.` · then, large: `WHEN WILL IT BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk kindly to your mind. Sit, and let it do what it does. When it wanders, and it will, don't snap at it. Speak to it the way you'd speak to a restless friend in the passenger seat: there you are, come back now. Or just: this breath. Talaputa scolded and coaxed. Try only the coaxing today. Notice whether a kind voice brings the mind home faster than a hard one. No need to decide. Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Kada. When: the word Talaputa the actor-turned-monk asks again and again, speaking to his own restless mind. Today's word.
Your line: when will it be. Today, the next time you catch yourself waiting, ask the question kindly, then come back to what's in front of you. Day eight hundred two.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in several Buddhist traditions encourage students to meet a wandering mind with patience rather than harshness, and some point to Talaputa's song as an early example of speaking to one's own mind.

myth: Talaputa's song is spoken to the Buddha all the way through
for much of it he speaks to his own mind, as if it sat across from him.
before he became a monk, Talaputa led a troupe of actors
in a sutta he asks the Buddha about actors, weeps at the answer, and asks to go forth.
in his song he only scolds the mind
he also reasons with it and coaxes it.

fork.setup: you're Talaputa, a monk now, and your mind keeps pulling back toward the old life. what do you do?
options: speak to the mind directly: scold it, reason with it, coax it.
fork.reveal: his song turns into a conversation with his own mind, part scolding, part coaxing. he doesn't deny it, and he doesn't simply obey it.

original.note: Pali: kada, when. Talaputa's question, asked over and over.

trapdoor: what you thought: an actor missing the stage.
what it means: Talaputa longs for the forest life, and argues with his own restless mind to get there.
what a scholar hears: the song is built on kada, when, repeated; then the speaker plays both parts, the monk and the mind.
recall: a name that sounds like full
foremost among nuns in psychic power

notes: SN 42.2 summary: Talaputa, headman of actors, asks whether actors who entertain with truth and falsehood are reborn among the 'laughing gods'; the Buddha declines twice, then answers; Talaputa weeps (the sutta says because he was deceived by earlier teachers) and goes forth. The script compresses this to 'weeps, and asks to go forth'. Confirm the compression is fair.

Thag 19.1 (vv. 1091–1145 as remembered): the run of 'when will I...' (kada) questions; later addressing the mind, including that the mind once urged him to go forth; references to forest, rain and birds (peacocks). Confirm each detail, especially 'you're the one who urged me into this life'.
'One man playing two parts' is offered as some readers' reading, not as the text's claim.
Original: कदा (kada); confirm Devanagari and stress.
Editor: 'half-truths' changed to 'truth and lies' to match SN 42.2's 'truth and falsehood'.

Auditor (fresh review): cut 'his when never quite turns into now' (the Theragatha counts Talaputa among the freed elders, so the line overstated the poem), and cut the unsourced 'unusual' and 'out loud'.
